kurz: How the CAPM derives the expected return of an investment from its beta, why it has largely failed empirically and why it nevertheless appears in every German valuation report.

bloecke.md:
Markowitz answers the question of which mixes are efficient. For a single investment, the question of what return you can demand from it remains open. Sharpe, Lintner and Mossin provided an answer in the mid-1960s. Their model, the CAPM, appears in practically every German valuation report, but has failed empirically in essential respects.

The derivation is short. If all investors hold the same risky mix and control their risk only through the share of the risk-free investment, then in equilibrium this mix must be the market itself. Every security is held in some portfolio, and the sum of all portfolios is the overall market. An investor who holds the market portfolio has diversified away all the risk that can be diversified away. With an individual share, they now bear only the part of its risk that moves with the market. The market pays no premium for the remaining part, because no investor has to bear it.

bloecke.erklaerung: The expected return of an investment is made up of the risk-free rate and a multiple of the market risk premium. This multiple is the investment's beta. Characteristics of the investment that are unrelated to the market do not appear in the equation.
variablen: Cov(Ri, Rm) / Var(Rm) = ρim × σi / σm
market risk premium, the price of one unit of market risk
bloecke.beispiel: German valuation practice in 2025 works with a risk-free base rate (Basiszins) of 2.5% and a market risk premium of 6.7 percentage points. With these values and a beta of 1.36, the cost of equity comes to 2.5 + 1.36 × 6.7 = 11.6% p.a.

bloecke.md:
## Components of beta

The second way of writing it, β = ρ × σi/σm, shows that two quantities interact, namely relative volatility and co-movement with the market. An investment can fluctuate strongly and still have a beta below one if its fluctuations have their own causes, independent of the market.

Emerging markets are an example of this. The annual euro returns from 2001 to 2025 give a standard deviation of 24.4% for the MSCI Emerging Markets and 17.7% for the MSCI World. The correlation between the two series, however, is only 0.69. The beta is therefore 0.69 × 24.4 / 17.7 = 0.95, and thus below one. According to the CAPM, the more volatile index is therefore the more defensive addition for an investor with a world portfolio, because the model rewards the contribution to the risk of the overall portfolio and not the risk of the investment on its own.

Volatility measures how strongly an investment fluctuates. Beta measures what part of this fluctuation it shares with the market. According to the CAPM, only this shared part is rewarded. The **coefficient of determination R²** indicates how meaningful an estimated beta is. For the DAX against the MSCI World it is 0.76 over 38 years, for emerging markets only 0.48.

bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation with a base rate of 2.5% and a market risk premium of 6.7 percentage points (KPMG cost of capital study 2025); the betas shown are back-calculated from the sectors' reported cost of equity.

bloecke.md:
## Assumptions of the model

The derivation rests on a series of assumptions: all investors optimise over the same single period according to expected value and variance, they have identical expectations, nobody moves the price with their order, there are no taxes and no transaction costs, all securities are infinitely divisible, and everyone can invest and borrow unlimited amounts at the risk-free rate.

The last assumption is particularly important, because its violation explains the deviation on which the model fails empirically. The assumption that there are no taxes is especially far from reality for German investors. Price gains, dividends and interest are taxed at 26.375%, and the partial exemption (Teilfreistellung) of 30% applies only to equity funds. German valuation practice therefore also calculates a variant after personal taxes, for which a separate, lower range for the market risk premium applies.

bloecke.titel: Roll's critique of the market portfolio
bloecke.md: The theoretical market portfolio contains every risky asset, that is, all the world's shares, bonds, property, unlisted companies and, in the limiting case, human capital as well. In practice, measurements are made against the S&P 500, the MSCI World or the DAX instead. In 1977 Richard Roll concluded from this that every test of the CAPM is a joint test. Such a test examines the model and the proxy index at the same time, and a negative result leaves open which of the two has failed. The same applies to every beta in a data sheet, because it is always a beta against a particular index.

## Estimating beta

A beta cannot simply be read off. It is estimated as the slope of a regression of the investment's return on the market return. Four decisions go into the estimate, each of which changes the result: the data frequency (daily, weekly, monthly), the length of the window, the reference index and the currency. Estimated betas tend to revert towards one over time. Some data services therefore report a smoothed beta following the Blume convention, which weights the raw value at two-thirds and the value one at one-third. Before comparing two betas, you should therefore check whether both were calculated using the same method.

With the same data, different windows produce different betas.

bloecke.titel: Beta of the DAX against the MSCI World, annual returns in euros
Rolling ten-year beta of the DAX against the MSCI World
bloecke.unter: Own regression, each over ten calendar-year returns in euros, with the year marking the end of the window; the measured values lie between 0.82 and 1.32.

bloecke.md:
The most recent window (2016-2025) produces a beta of 0.82 with a standard error of 0.21. The band of two standard errors around the estimate therefore ranges from about 0.40 to 1.24.

With a base rate of 2.5% and a market risk premium of 6.7 percentage points, the point estimate gives a cost of equity of 2.5 + 0.82 × 6.7 = 8.0%. Within the band, 2.5 + 0.40 × 6.7 = 5.2% is just as possible as 2.5 + 1.24 × 6.7 = 10.8%. In a present value model, these values lead to completely different company valuations.

## Alpha as a residual

Jensen's [[Alpha|alpha]] is a residual, calculated as α = Ri − [Rf + β × (Rm − Rf)]. It measures by how much the return of an investment lay above or below the line implied by its beta. As a residual, alpha contains all the dispersion that the model does not explain, which is why it is so hard to prove.

For the DAX against the MSCI World, alpha over the period from 1988 to 2025 is around +0.8 percentage points a year. The standard error of this value is 2.0 percentage points, which puts the t-statistic at 0.39, so the alpha cannot be statistically distinguished from zero. The dispersion of the annual deviations is 11.0 percentage points. To establish one percentage point of alpha statistically (t = 2) with this residual dispersion, you would need around (2 × 11 / 1)² ≈ 484 annual observations. No fund manager and no index has such a long data series, and no investor can wait that long.

bloecke.md:
## Empirical deviations from the model

The best-known finding is the **low-beta anomaly**. Historically, shares with a low beta delivered at least market-like returns with considerably lower risk, and shares with a high beta delivered less than the line promises. The observed security market line is therefore too flat. Black, as well as Haugen and Heins, documented this as early as 1972. Frazzini and Pedersen (Journal of Financial Economics 2014) find the line too flat in 18 of the 19 international equity markets they studied, and also in bonds, credit and futures.

Their explanation starts from the assumption that everyone can borrow unlimited amounts at the risk-free rate. According to the model, an investor who wants more return than the market offers would have to buy the market on credit. For many investors, this is prohibited (fund regulation, investment guidelines) or uncomfortable. Instead, they buy high-beta shares, drive up their prices and thereby lower their future returns. This additional demand makes the premium for high beta disappear. Other explanations are the preference for securities with lottery-like characteristics, benchmark incentives for fund managers and overconfidence.

There are also dissenting voices. In 2022, in a paper entitled *Betting Against Betting Against Beta*, Novy-Marx and Velikov show that a large part of the measured premium depends on the unusual construction of the original study. It weights by inverse beta and as a result heavily overweights very small caps. With conventional weighting and after transaction costs, the effect shrinks considerably. In addition, Fama and French have found that a single factor is not enough. For diversified US portfolios, their five-factor model explains over 90% of the variation in returns, the CAPM around 70%.

punkte: The division into diversifiable and non-diversifiable risk is correct regardless of the model.
The market rewards a security's contribution to portfolio risk, but not its individual fluctuation.
Beta and alpha provide a language in which excess return can be discussed precisely.
Beta is linear in the weights and can therefore easily be aggregated at portfolio level.
The observed security market line is flatter than the theoretical one.
One factor is not enough, because size, value, profitability and momentum explain additional parts of returns.
Beta changes over time, and the estimate depends on the window, frequency and reference index.
The market portfolio is not observable, so every test also tests the proxy index.

bloecke.md:
## The CAPM in German valuation practice

In Germany, business valuation follows the IDW S1 standard, under which the cost of equity is estimated with the CAPM. The base rate is derived from the Bundesbank's Svensson yield curve and does not correspond to the yield of a German federal bond on a given day. The calculation has direct practical consequences. In squeeze-outs, domination agreements (Beherrschungsverträge) and the appraisal proceedings (Spruchverfahren) that follow them, the amount of cash compensation depends on the three inputs of the equation.

The KPMG cost of capital study 2025 shows which values are used in practice. It covers around 300 companies, including over 230 German companies and 65% of the DAX 40 constituents. The study reports a base rate of 2.5%, a market risk premium of 6.7 percentage points, an average levered beta of 1.03, an average cost of equity of 9.7% and an average WACC of 8.5%.

bloecke.titel: Cost of capital by sector (KPMG study 2025, Germany, Austria, Switzerland)
Dispute over the market risk premium
bloecke.md: Two cross-checks show how uncertain the inputs are. First, 2.5 + 1.03 × 6.7 comes to 9.4% arithmetically, but 9.7% is reported. The study averages each quantity separately across the figures provided by the companies surveyed. Since these do not all calculate with the same values, the formula applied to the averages does not produce the reported mean. Second, German practice assumes a market risk premium of 6.7 percentage points, whereas Damodaran reports an implied total equity risk premium of 4.23% for Germany at the beginning of 2026 (country risk premium Germany 0.00; Italy 2.46, Brazil 3.24). The two figures do not measure the same quantity. One is implied from prices and cash flow expectations, while the other is based on historical returns and on the recommendation of the Institute of Public Auditors in Germany (IDW), a professional body. With a beta of 1.3, there is nevertheless a gap of around 3.2 percentage points in the cost of equity between them. In addition, the yield on ten-year Bunds was 3.52% on 18 September 2026, just over one percentage point above the base rate used in the 2025 study.

The beta of a portfolio is the weighted average of the individual betas: βp = Σ wi × βi. This does not apply to the variance of a portfolio, because it also contains covariance terms. This is the practical advantage of beta as a metric.

An example: 70% world ETF (β = 1.0), 20% instant-access savings account (β = 0) and 10% DAX ETF (β = 1.02). The portfolio beta is 0.70 + 0 + 0.102 = 0.80. With a base rate of 2.5% and a premium of 6.7 percentage points, the CAPM expects 2.5 + 0.80 × 6.7 = 7.9% p.a.

A higher low-risk allocation lowers beta proportionally. This reflects Tobin separation, according to which the selection of securities and the dosing of risk are two separate decisions.

mitnehmen: The CAPM rewards only the risk that cannot be diversified away, and beta measures the contribution to this market risk rather than the fluctuation on its own, which is why an index can fluctuate more strongly and still have a beta below one.
Beta is an estimate with a wide confidence band, because the rolling ten-year beta of the DAX against the MSCI World lay between 0.82 and 1.32, and individual windows reach a standard error of 0.33.

Alpha is a residual and contains all the unexplained dispersion, so with a residual dispersion of 11 percentage points a year you would need centuries of data to establish one percentage point of alpha.
Empirically, the security market line is too flat, because low-beta shares deliver more return and high-beta shares less than the model predicts.
German valuation practice under IDW S1 nevertheless works with this equation; in appraisal proceedings, the base rate, the market risk premium and beta are regularly disputed.

begriffe.text: The covariance of an investment with the market divided by the variance of the market, which equals the correlation times the ratio of the standard deviations. Beta measures the contribution to market risk, not the total fluctuation. By definition, the market has a beta of 1.

Graphical representation of the CAPM with expected return on the vertical axis and beta on the horizontal axis. The line starts at the risk-free rate and rises with the market risk premium. Empirically, the observed line is flatter than the theoretical one.

Deviation of the realised return from the CAPM prediction, calculated as α = Ri − [Rf + β × (Rm − Rf)]. As a residual, alpha contains all the unexplained dispersion, which is why a very large number of observations is needed to prove it statistically.
The part of an investment's fluctuation that is related to the overall market and cannot be eliminated through diversification. According to the CAPM, only this part is rewarded with a risk premium.

Empirical finding that low-beta shares deliver higher risk-adjusted returns than the CAPM predicts, and high-beta shares lower ones. Explanations include borrowing constraints, the preference for securities with lottery-like characteristics and benchmark incentives.
